title: Zacchaeus gives back
hook: a hated tax collector is welcomed, and gives back fourfold (Luke 19:1–10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crowd that walked away one by one. Your line was put down the stone. Which judgment did you drop? Today, the end of the week, and forgiveness seen from the other side: the one who did the wrong. Day nine hundred fifty-two.

Jericho, and the streets are packed because Jesus is passing through. Somewhere at the back of the crowd is a rich man who can't see a thing. Luke gives us his name, Zacchaeus, his job, chief among the tax collectors, and one more detail: he was little of stature. So he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree to watch from the branches. Jesus reaches the spot, stops, looks up, and calls him by name. Today: Zacchaeus gives back.
screen: `A CROWD TOO TALL TO SEE OVER.` → `A RICH MAN UP A TREE.` → `CALLED BY NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. In the King James words, Jesus says: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Not a lecture. Jesus invites himself to the man's house. And Zacchaeus comes down fast and receives him joyfully. Second, the grumbling. Luke says that when people saw it, they all murmured that he had gone to be a guest with a man that is a sinner. The welcome comes first, before any change, and the crowd doesn't like it. Third, the turn. Zacchaeus stands up and says: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Fourfold. Not an apology alone. Not just giving back what he took. Four times over. Nobody demands this of him in the story. It pours out of him once he's been welcomed. Fourth, the answer. Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house," and adds, "the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost." Some readers notice the order here. The welcome came before the repair, and the repair was real and costly. Forgiveness, in this story, doesn't cancel making it right. It sets it free. And that closes the week. We cast crumbs on the water with Tashlich, heard trespasses in the Lord's Prayer, learned from Peter's question, watched the servant forget the talents he'd been forgiven, heard Father, forgive them, and saw a crowd put down its stones. Zacchaeus adds the last piece: the one who has been welcomed gives back more than he took.
screen: `COME DOWN: TODAY, AT THY HOUSE.` · `THE CROWD MURMURS.` · `HALF TO THE POOR, FOURFOLD BACK.` · `WELCOME FIRST, THEN REPAIR.` · then, large: `I RESTORE HIM FOURFOLD.`

segments.voice: Lower your eyes, and let the breath slow. This time, turn the story around. Find one old wrong you did. Something small enough to name, and old enough that it's been quietly sitting there. A loan never repaid. A credit you took. A friend you dropped. Don't punish yourself. Just look at it squarely, the way Zacchaeus named his own dealings. Then ask: what would giving it back look like? Not just even. A little more than even. Let one concrete step come to mind. If you pray, you can hold that step in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Zacchaeus. The tax collector Jesus welcomed to dinner, who then promised half his goods to the poor and fourfold to anyone he had cheated. Today's word.
Your line: fourfold. Today, take one step to repay an old wrong, and make it a little more generous than it has to be. Day nine hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Christians read the story of Zacchaeus as a picture of welcome leading to repentance and restitution.

notes: Week end (days 946–952): the teach closes by naming the week. Day 946 (Tashlich) was not on disk when this was written; its title comes from the outline.
KJV spells the tree 'sycomore' (Luke 19:4); the voice says sycamore in its own words, not as a quotation.
KJV calls Zacchaeus 'chief among the publicans'; the voice says 'tax collectors' in its own words.
Readers differ on whether Luke 19:8's verbs describe a new promise or Zacchaeus's existing practice; the voice follows the common reading of a promise. A Keeper may want to note the other reading.
